newsitem.title: UK: BT to prove global plans won't hurt UK users.
newsitem.headline: BT to prove global plans won't hurt UK users.

text.p: British Telecommunications Plc's regulator told the company on Thursday to submit a certificate every year to prove that it does not neglect British customers in its drive for global expansion.

BT's $20 billion plans to merge with MCI Communications Corp, America's second biggest long-distance operator, have underscored the issue after MCI announced an unexpected profit warning two weeks ago.

But MCI is far from BT's only foreign investment. It is involved in over 70 other joint ventures and overseas distribution deals across more than 40 countries. It also plans to break into the lucrative Asia Pacific region.

BT announced on Thursday that its Italian venture, called Albacom, would be enhanced after Italian energy group Eni joined to take a 35 percent stake -- and offer its national fibre optic network for use.
But the British telecoms giant says that gaining access to the vast but competitive U.S. telephone market remains a vital part of its global strategy.

The BT-MCI merger to create one of the world's biggest, global telecoms alliances called Concert Plc had been trumpeted as the largest trans-Atlantic merger in history which would yield "tremendous growth prospects".

But the deal ended its eight-month honeymoon two weeks ago after MCI said it was finding it harder, more expensive and more time-consuming to enter U.S. local phone markets. It was also looking at hefty losses.

As top BT directors launch a thorough review of the MCI's businesses, telecoms watchdog Oftel said it would add a condition to BT's licence to ensure that the phone giant meets obligations to customers and rivals at home.
BT will be prohibited from doing anything which could jeopardise its ability to provide and finance telecoms services for its British customers.
Oftel director general Don Cruickshank said that although the risk of BT spending too much management time or resources on overseas expansion plans was small, it was a risk that could not be ignored.
Cruickshank noted that events since the publication in March of his last consultative document had highlighted the need for "extra regulatory vigilance".
"The measures I have announced today are designed to provide the additional regulatory reassurance necessary while permitting BT to pursue its interests globally," he stated.
MCI's surprise news of around $1.3 billion of unforeseen losses over the next 18 months sent shares plunging and triggered calls for BT to renegotiate merger terms or even walk away from the deal.
BT, which has ruled nothing out amid concern that MCI's core business might also be damaged, declines to comment on the future of what would have been the largest transatlantic merger on record.
But it insists it can legally protect shareholders from any financial compensation MCI might demand if the current deal does not go ahead as planned.
"We are continuing to look into the matter," a company spokesman said. "Obviously it is a very complex situation."
Oliver Ehrenberg, telecoms analyst at brokers Robert Fleming -- one of the most bearish brokers on the MCI deal -- warns MCI will prove to be a black hole for BT.
MCI's profit warning in local telephony, he argues, is only the tip of the iceberg because MCI is dangerously playing down difficulties in its core long-distance market.

MCI's arch-rival AT&T Corp, America's biggest long-distance carrier, has already posted 36 percent lower quarterly earnings, partly because of rising competition in the U.S. long-distance market. Given this trend, MCI's own forecasts of flat earnings in its core business were "highly optimistic", Ehrenberg said.
"BT should seize the current opportunity and cancel the deal," he said.
BT's shares were trading five pence weaker at 425p at 1245 GMT -- substantially below their year high of 504p.
